item.title: Free tiers are a design constraint, not a discount
item.dc:creator: anuj
item.content:encoded:
Three production platforms, no infrastructure bill. That sounds like a procurement story and it isn't. Treating a free tier as a permanent requirement rather than a temporary discount changes the architecture, and it changes it in ways that are mostly good — the same pressure that keeps the bill at zero also keeps the system small.

The systems below are real and running. Where a number appears, it was measured; where a vendor limit appears, check it yourself before relying on it, because pricing pages move faster than blog posts.

The integrations, and why each one was chosen

The two exceptions are worth naming rather than hiding. Kite Connect is a paid subscription: there is no free tier for placing real orders, and pretending otherwise would be the sort of claim that gets someone's budget wrong. Google Routes is billed per call, and the interesting engineering was bounding it rather than avoiding it.

Running the LLM layer on free models

This is the part people assume cannot work in production, so it is the part worth the most detail.

Shubh Bhagya's readings, horoscopes and question answering all run on Groq's free tier against open-weight gpt-oss models. Not a trial, not a fallback for when the paid key runs out — that is the production path.

The provider chain is an ordered, comma-separated list, currently two entries pointing at different-sized gpt-oss models. The order is shuffled per request so load spreads across them, and the chain falls through on failure, so a single provider having a bad minute degrades latency instead of returning an error.

Quotas are keyed per model, which is the whole trick

The single most useful fact here:

Groq's quotas are keyed per model, so listing several distinct models multiplies effective throughput on one API key.

And the trap that comes with it: listing two chain entries that resolve to the same model does nothing. They share one bucket while looking like extra capacity — the config appears to have doubled your headroom and has not. That failure is silent, and it is only visible if you know quotas are per-model rather than per-key.

One model had to be thrown out, and the measurement is why

A third model — a 27B Qwen variant — was removed from the chain deliberately. It rejects the reasoning_effort parameter with a 400, which makes it the one model in the set that cannot be bounded. Unbounded, it reasons until it hits the completion limit, gets truncated mid-thought, and the envelope stripper cleans the partial reasoning down to zero visible characters. A forty-second call returning nothing.

The cost was measurable at the job level: the full two-language horoscope run took 399 seconds with that model in the chain, and 213 seconds without it.

That is the argument for keeping a chain configurable rather than clever. The fix was one entry removed from a list.

Two rules that came out of production

Bound the reasoning, and output gets better, not worse. Setting reasoning_effort="low" cut completion tokens by roughly 85% on the larger model, 3,072 down to about 302, and increased the visible output, because less of the budget was spent on reasoning that gets stripped before the reader sees it. Capability is probed at runtime rather than hardcoded: a model that 400s on the parameter is remembered and retried without it. Hardcoded model lists go stale: two entries in this chain once pointed at decommissioned models, and nobody noticed until the daily job ran out of quota.

An empty completion is an error, not an answer. The call raises rather than returning an empty string. Before that, a response consisting only of stripped reasoning was indistinguishable from success — and a blank reading got cached and served for a full day.

Prefix caching is not the saving you think

About 96% of a horoscope prompt is a byte-identical prefix across the twelve signs — same instructions, same structure, different chart data at the end. That looks like an obvious prefix-caching win.

Measured, Groq's prefix caching hit 1 time in 6. It is opportunistic, not guaranteed, and a cost model that assumes it will hit is a cost model that is wrong five times out of six. Design as though every call is cold; treat a cache hit as a bonus.

A later measurement, on 2026-10-17, said the same thing more precisely: 1 hit in 7 identical calls, and 13.9% of prompt tokens actually saved.

The model will ignore your prompt occasionally

The readings render raw with no markdown filter, so any asterisk reaches the page. The prompt says not to emit markdown. Told not to, the model still emitted bold in 1 of 4 generations, so the rule is enforced by a stripper in code as well.

That ratio is worth internalising for anything user-facing: a prompt instruction is a strong prior, not a guarantee, and anything that must be true gets enforced after generation.

The constraint that shapes everything else

Shubh Bhagya's storage sits in the US because the Cloud Storage free tier is US-only. Its compute runs in Mumbai because that is where the readers are. Those two facts cannot both be optimised, so every bucket round-trip pays cross-continent latency, permanently.

That is a cost decision creating a latency tax, and it produced the single worst performance bug in the project: the homepage took roughly 13 seconds because it made about 30 sequential bucket round-trips per render.

The fix was not a bigger cache or a closer bucket. It was 32 storage operations to zero, taking the page under one second. When a dependency is expensive by construction, the move is to stop calling it, not to call it faster.

Scale-to-zero is the other half of the same trade. minScale: 0 means paying nothing while idle and accepting cold starts as the literal price — a deliberate choice rather than an oversight, and the sort of thing that should be written down so nobody "fixes" it later.

Bounding the API that does cost money

VeoCabs needs road distances between arbitrary Indian cities, and Google Routes bills per call. An agent-facing or bot-crawled quote endpoint is an unbounded bill waiting to happen.

Distance resolution therefore goes through three tiers before anything is billed: curated routes answer from a table, anything else checks a cache in Postgres, and only a genuine miss reaches Google — with the result written back immediately. The cache key is the two endpoints sorted, so Delhi→Jaipur and Jaipur→Delhi are one entry rather than two.

The effect is that cost is bounded by the number of distinct city pairs anyone has ever asked for, rather than by traffic. A route that goes viral is billed once. That property comes entirely from the shape of the cache key.

Email and alerts, chosen on quota

Transactional email runs on Brevo, and the reason recorded in the code is refreshingly unsentimental: the free tier covers 300 emails a day with no card required. SendGrid and Mailgun would work equally well — Brevo simply won on quota at the time the choice was made. (That number is from the integration's own notes; re-check it before you plan around it.)

Operator alerts go to Telegram rather than email, because the operator already lives in it and replies in seconds. The design detail that matters more than the channel: if Telegram is unconfigured or unreachable, the enquiry is logged and the submission still returns success. A lead is worth more than a notification — failing the form to protect a side effect loses the customer.

What it actually costs you

Free is not free, and pretending otherwise is how people get burned.

  • Cold starts, as the price of scale-to-zero.
  • Cross-continent latency, permanently, because the free region and the users are not in the same place.
  • Model quality below the frontier. Open-weight gpt-oss models are not the best available. For prose written about data that was already computed deterministically, they are comfortably good enough — but that only holds because the hard reasoning was moved into code first. Free models are viable in production largely to the extent that you have narrowed what the model has to do.
  • Vendor lock to whoever's free tier you built around, which is real, and mitigated here only because the provider chain is a config string.

The compensation is that every one of those pressures pushes toward a smaller system: fewer network calls, more caching, less work handed to the model, and constraints written down where the next person will find them.

Cost discipline turns out to be architectural discipline wearing a different hat.

If you need an AI product to run in production on a budget close to zero, that is the kind of build I take on; Shubh Bhagya and VeoCabs are the two systems this post draws on.
item.excerpt:encoded: What changes when zero infrastructure spend is a hard requirement — including running a consumer product's LLM layer entirely on free open-weight models, and the measurements that made it work.

item.title: When the API places real orders
item.dc:creator: anuj
item.content:encoded:
Most integrations fail cheaply. A rate limit returns 429, you back off, nobody notices. A webhook drops, you replay it.

A brokerage API is not that. It runs 9:15 to 15:30 IST1 against a real account with real money, and every defect has a price: a duplicate order, a position that never squared off, a signal that fired into a window nobody was watching. The daemon behind VivaTrades' intraday side does exactly this, and almost none of the interesting engineering is the strategy.

The failure modes worth designing against

Before any of the mechanics, it is worth being precise about what can actually go wrong, because it is a short and specific list:

Notice what is not on that list: strategy quality. A bad signal loses a predictable, bounded amount. A duplicate order loses an unbounded one, and it does it while you are asleep.

Rate limits are a design input, not an error handler

Kite's limits are roughly 10 requests per second and 3,000 per day for order-related calls. Those numbers are generous for a strategy that acts a handful of times a day and immediately hostile to a tight loop.

The important consequence is architectural rather than defensive: a daily cap means a retry storm can exhaust the budget for the session. Burning 3,000 calls by 11am does not degrade the system gracefully — it leaves open positions with no ability to place the orders that would close them. The rate limit stops being a throughput concern and becomes a liveness one: whether the system can still act at all.

So the review checklist for anything touching this code asks about tight loops around placeOrder before it asks about anything else, and every placeOrder / modifyOrder / cancelOrder has to carry explicit error handling. A silent .catch(() => {}) is the specific pattern that turns a rejected order into a position you believe you closed.

The clock is the hard dependency

Three timers govern the session, and each exists because a specific thing breaks without it:

  • 08:30 — token check. Kite access tokens expire every morning before the market opens, and a fresh one needs a login. A daemon that discovers a stale token at 09:15 has already missed the open. Checking early and alerting on Telegram means the failure lands 45 minutes before it matters, while a human can still act.
  • 09:12 to 15:15 — scan every 3 minutes. The loop starts before the market opens rather than at the bell.
  • 15:15 — square off. Intraday positions left open become a settlement problem, so this is the one deadline the system genuinely cannot miss.

The scan cadence is driven by an interval timer, and the loop carries an explicit in-flight guard: if a scan is still running when the next tick arrives, the tick logs scan already in progress and returns. Without that, a slow scan quietly becomes two concurrent scans looking at the same signals and reaching the same conclusions twice.

Overlap protection matters more here than in an ordinary job queue. Two concurrent scans do not just waste work — they can independently decide the same entry is valid, and the deduplication that saves you has to exist downstream of both.

Alerting is part of the trading path, but must never block it

Every meaningful event goes to Telegram: token expiry, order placement, the square-off result, and errors with the specifics attached. That last part is the difference between a useful alert and a notification — closed N open MIS positions at 15:15 can be checked; square-off completed cannot.

The rule that makes it safe: an alert failing must never stop trading. If Telegram is unreachable, the daemon carries on and the failure surfaces elsewhere. Wiring a notification channel into the critical path means an outage at a messaging provider becomes an outage in your trading system, which is a spectacular way to lose money to something irrelevant.

The heartbeat follows the same logic in the opposite direction. The daemon POSTs every two minutes, and a failure to post is deliberately silent locally — because the point of a heartbeat is that something else notices its absence. A process that alerts on its own failure to report is solving the easy half of the problem.

Restart is the question that matters

This is the question I would ask first of any system like this, and here it is still open.

If the daemon crashes between placing an order and recording that it placed one, what happens on restart? PM2 will bring the process back.2 If the process reconstructs its intent from the same signals, it may place the order again.

The two standard answers are an idempotency key — Kite's tag field, set deterministically so a repeat is recognisably the same order — or a local order ledger written before the call, so a restart can reconcile what it intended against what the broker actually holds.

The daemon tracks entries and exits in memory to avoid duplicate alerts, and that is a different guarantee: it dedupes what you are told, not what is placed, and it does not survive a restart. Reconstructing from the broker's own order book at startup is the version that does.

This is exactly why the review agent for this code exists and why its checklist leads with idempotency. A checklist is most valuable where the answer is not yet "yes". Encoding the question in a reviewer that runs on every change to these files is how it stays asked, rather than being noticed once and forgotten.

Square-off deserves its own paranoia

The 15:15 deadline has failure modes the rest of the session does not:

  • Partial fills. If a position is 100 and 60 fill, the remaining 40 is an overnight position nobody decided to hold. The alert has to say the remainder, not just report that a square-off ran.
  • Timing collision. If the daemon is mid-scan at 15:15, the square-off needs priority over more signal evaluation. Entering a new intraday position at 15:14 is a bug with a same-day cost.
  • Failure alerting. A failed square-off is the single most expensive silent failure available, so it alerts with symbol, quantity and remainder.

What generalises

Very little of this is about trading. The transferable parts:

  • Rate limits with a daily cap are a liveness concern. Budget them for the worst hour, not the average one, and remember that exhausting them can leave you unable to perform the closing action.
  • Alerting belongs beside the critical path, never inside it.
  • A heartbeat is only useful if something else watches for silence.
  • Ask what a restart does mid-operation, and prefer a durable record written before the side effect over any amount of in-memory bookkeeping.
  • Where the answer is "not yet", encode the question somewhere that runs automatically. An unanswered question in a checklist that executes beats a solved problem in someone's memory.

The general principle: when a bug costs money rather than a retry, the engineering effort moves from making the happy path good to making the interrupted path safe. Almost everything above is about the second one.

If you are connecting software, or an agent, to an API that moves money, I can review what a restart does to it before it runs unattended; the daemon above sits behind VivaTrades.

  1. IST is Indian Standard Time, UTC+05:30. Every time in this post is IST. ↩︎
  2. PM2 is the Node.js process manager the daemon runs under. It restarts a process that exits, but it knows nothing about orders. ↩︎
item.excerpt:encoded: A trading daemon runs unattended for six hours a day on a real brokerage account. The engineering that matters is not the strategy — it is what happens when something restarts at the wrong moment.

item.title: Governance theatre: auditing an AI support bot
item.dc:creator: anuj
item.content:encoded:
The analytics panel in ai-support-bot showed how many conversations were live. The number was Math.floor(Math.random() * 50) + 10.

Every answer also carried a confidence score. It was 85 whenever the answer drew on documents, and 95 if the answer ran past 200 characters.

Neither was a bug in the usual sense.

Governance theatre is a control that is displayed but does not exist: a panel, badge or score a reviewer can tick off with nothing behind it. The check that matters most is to follow every displayed control to the code path that implements it, then confirm that code is what is actually deployed.

Updated to the repository at commit 6e91402 (2026-10-25). The numbered sections describe what the audit found and how each finding was fixed. What it does now covers what was built afterwards.

What is ai-support-bot?

ai-support-bot turns uploaded documents into a support assistant that can be embedded on any website. Upload TXT, Markdown, PDF or DOCX files, chat with them in a preview, then paste a script tag into your own site.

It is a Next.js app built on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): for each question it finds the most relevant passages in the uploaded documents and hands them to a language model to answer from. Passages are matched using embeddings, lists of numbers that place text with similar meaning close together.

The previous post, on governing a read-only MCP server, put an MCP server through five questions a company asks before letting an AI tool near its data:

  1. What can it actually do?
  2. What stops it doing more?
  3. Where does the data go?
  4. Are the outputs what they claim to be?
  5. Is there a record of what happened?

mcp-zerodha was well behaved and still failed four. This one failed all five. The landing page promised an enterprise panel with an audit log, single sign-on, real-time analytics and a confidence score on every answer. None of the four was backed by code that did what the screen said.

What the audit found

1. A route that could read and wipe everything

src/app/api/debug/route.ts answered GET with every session, every document, the session-to-document mappings and the first 200 characters of sample chunks. POST with clearDatabase: true emptied the store. Neither checked who was asking, and its CORS preflight answered any origin.

A debug route is a normal thing to write during development. The governance failure is that nothing distinguished it from the product, so it shipped with the product.

It is deleted, and the check in GOVERNANCE.md is that GET /api/debug returns 404.

2. Nothing bounded what a caller could do

The same commit closes three more holes, all in code that took input from anyone on the internet.

The upload path came from the uploaded filename. The temp file was built like this:

const tempFileName = `upload-${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).substring(7)}-${file.name}`
const tempFilePath = path.join(tempDir, tempFileName)

A file named ../../x wrote outside the temp directory, and the cleanup step then deleted whatever was at that path. The name now plays no part in the path:

const extension = path.extname(path.basename(file.name)).toLowerCase()
const safeExtension = ['.txt', '.md', '.pdf', '.docx'].includes(extension) ? extension : ''
const tempFilePath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `upload-${crypto.randomUUID()}${safeExtension}`)

IDs came from Math.random. That matters here more than usual. There are no accounts, so a session ID is the only thing between a stranger and a session's documents: it is a bearer secret, usable by whoever holds it. Math.random is not a cryptographic generator, and its output is predictable. Session IDs and widget keys now come from crypto.randomUUID().

Nothing limited spending. Every chat request spends the deployment's model quota, and the widget routes accept requests from any site. That is the risk OWASP calls unbounded consumption.

A new src/lib/guard.ts adds a per-IP limit (20 chats and 10 uploads a minute). It caps messages at 2,000 characters and custom system prompts, the instructions sent to the model ahead of the conversation, at 4,000. It also checks a widget's allowed_domains against the browser's Origin header, a field that had been stored but never read.

These are limits with stated edges. The rate counts live in memory, so each server instance keeps its own and a restart resets them. They are keyed on the client's IP as clientIp reads it from the x-real-ip and x-forwarded-for headers; on a host that passes those through from the client, a caller can change them on every request and get past the limit. The domain check stops another website embedding a widget, but not a script that forges the header. The builder never set allowed_domains; it now offers an exact-origin list instead (below). GOVERNANCE.md lists each of these as a known gap.

3. "Your data stays isolated"

The landing page said Secure and private, your data stays isolated. The README said Privacy First: your data stays isolated and secure.

Neither said where the data went. It went to OpenAI twice: once to embed every uploaded document, and again to answer every question. The retrieval code also logged the text of visitor questions.

Three changes, in order of what they buy:

  • Documents no longer leave the server to be indexed. Commit 014099d embeds them in-process with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 through transformers.js. The model weights are downloaded from Hugging Face on first use; that download sends no user data.
  • Logs record question length, not question text (9c2b096).
  • The slogan is replaced with a list. The builder shows a data disclosure, and GOVERNANCE.md says what stays on the server, what goes to the model provider (Groq by default), what sits in server memory and what reaches the browser.

The disclosure needed a correction of its own. The first version said the provider retained nothing by default. Commit 6fd93dd records that Groq's data-controls page says inputs and outputs may be stored for up to 30 days unless the organisation enables Zero Data Retention, and rewrites the disclosure to say that, with the setting to change.

A disclosure that understates retention is the same defect as the slogan, only more convincing.

4. The numbers were invented

This is the finding that gives the post its title.

The confidence score. Every answer carried a confidence field. In the widget route, the code computed a figure from retrieval similarity and then discarded it, because it returned response.confidence || confidence and the model call always set its own. That one was decided by this:

if (isEnhanced && context) {
  confidence = 85
  if (message.length > 200) {
    confidence = Math.min(95, confidence + 10)
  }
}

So any answer that drew on documents scored 85, and 95 if it ran past 200 characters. Without documents it was 30, or 35 if the answer contained words like specific or documentation. Length is not evidence of anything. A long, wrong answer scored highest. A score like that invites the overreliance described in LLM09: Misinformation.

Neither widget script displayed the field, a correction GOVERNANCE.md records against its own earlier wording, but any API client could read it.

It now carries a retrieval match score, from matchScore in src/lib/embeddings.ts. That is where the best passage's cosine similarity sits between two cut-offs, on a 0 to 100 scale, and 0 when no passage was used. The UI labels it a match score. It measures how closely a passage matches the question, not whether the answer is correct, and the docs say exactly that.

The cut-offs had to be measured. Switching embedding models changed the similarity scale. Against the repo's own faq.md, passages that answer a question scored 0.18 to 0.57 with the new model; the best passage for an unrelated question scored under 0.10. The old retrieval started its search at a 0.5 threshold, which sits near the top of the new range.

MIN_SIMILARITY is now 0.15 and STRONG_SIMILARITY 0.5, in one file, with a comment saying to re-measure before changing the model. GOVERNANCE.md is plain that this is calibrated on one document.

The analytics and the customers. The analytics route returned Math.floor(Math.random() * 50) + 10 active conversations, a random average confidence between 0.85 and 0.95, and so on. The enterprise panel showed SSO logins and audit-event counts from the same source, and enabling SSO wrote a line to the console.

The landing page said Join thousands of companies, 90% query accuracy and 50% support cost reduction, and listed a support address on a domain the project does not own. Commit 80908c7 removes all of it: 1,740 lines deleted, eleven added.

A fabricated metric is worse than a missing one. A reviewer who sees no analytics asks for them. A reviewer who sees plausible analytics moves on, and the product has answered a governance question with a random number.

5. The audit log never ran

The enterprise panel had an audit log. According to the commit that removed it, the page passed a business ID the lookup did not recognise, so it never returned anything real.

The fix was deletion, not implementation. At 6e91402 there is still no per-request audit record beyond server diagnostics, and the post would be its own kind of theatre if it said otherwise.

Two quieter changes belong under the same question, because a record is only useful if failures show up in it:

  • Embedding errors used to return zero vectors. On failure the old code returned new Array(1536).fill(0), stored the document anyway and reported the upload as a success. A zero vector matches nothing, so the bot silently knew less than its owner thought. Embedding failures now throw.
  • Chat errors used to return a canned answer. When the model call failed, the bot replied I don't have access to your specific information. Could you provide more details… with a confidence of 10, which reads like a working bot being unhelpful. It now returns an error.

6. The fixes were not live

Everything above was committed and pushed. None of it was running.

Commit a11ed4c records that every production deploy since 2026-08-30 had been blocked by Vercel's check for a vulnerable Next.js version, so the live site was still the build from 2025-08-01. The commits after the upgrade fix four more failures that only existed in production:

  • The default chat model, llama-3.1-8b-instant, had been shut down by Groq on 2026-08-16, so chat returned 404 (d4aeaab). The same day's migration to Groq had chosen that model.
  • The functions were missing the native ONNX runtime the embeddings need, and once included, pulled in about 260 MB of CUDA providers that took them past Vercel's 250 MB limit (d4aeaab, 4c8949c).
  • pdf-parse runs a self-test when it is not the main module, which is always true once bundled, so every PDF upload failed with ENOENT (08fe1da).
  • The embed code pointed at the per-deployment URL, which sits behind Vercel's login and changes on every deploy, so pasted widgets could not reach the API (db15260).

None of these is a governance control. All of them decide whether the controls exist anywhere but the repository. A review of the code answers what the code does. It does not answer what is running.

What it does now

After the audit, four features changed where data and credentials can go. Each arrived with its controls and its gaps written into GOVERNANCE.md.

Your own database. Merged in 67f7d5f. A builder step takes a Postgres connection string. Documents, passages, embeddings and widget settings then live in a support_bot schema in that database, with embeddings in a pgvector column. pgvector is a Postgres extension that stores embeddings and searches them by similarity. Every query is filtered to the workspace named in the token.

The server does not store the connection string. It is sealed into two tokens: a builder token kept in the browser's localStorage, and a widget token inside the embed code (5edeac8). Both are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a server key, EMBED_TOKEN_KEY. GCM is authenticated encryption, and the token's prefix is part of what is authenticated, so an edited or relabelled token fails to decrypt.

The repo also ships SQL for a least-privilege role, one with only the rights the app needs: SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the support_bot tables, no DELETE and no DDL (499df8a).

Until a database is connected, the builder says so: Demo: documents and this widget are deleted when the server restarts (68af660).

Your own model. Merged in c53498e. An owner can attach any OpenAI-compatible model with a base URL, API key and model ID; answers for their preview and embeds then come from it and spend their credits. The key reaches the browser and the embed code only inside encrypted tokens (2db727e).

Every call checks the model address first. It must be https:, and anything that resolves to localhost, a private network or a link-local address such as 169.254.169.254 is refused unless the operator opts in. That guards against server-side request forgery, where a caller makes the server reach internal addresses on their behalf (e1938a5). If the owner's model fails, the preview returns 502 and the widget 503; the answer never quietly comes from Groq instead.

Allowed sites. Merged in the same c53498e. The embed step takes up to 10 sites, normalised to scheme://host[:port] and matched exactly (80e3915). The widget chat route refuses an unlisted, missing or null Origin with 403 before any retrieval or model call. An embed that uses an owner model or a backend cannot be generated without at least one site, because it carries a credential that spends someone's money or reaches their server.

Your own backend. Merged in 6e91402. An owner can run a server that implements the repo's connector API, and the app then sends documents and questions to it and keeps no copy beyond each request. The repo includes a reference server in connector/, on Postgres and pgvector, with a Dockerfile and a Compose file (390c143, df8040f).

Every request after the first health check carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature, a keyed hash over the method, the path, a timestamp, a random nonce and the body's hash. In the QA run recorded in GOVERNANCE.md, the reference server refused tampered, stale and replayed requests with 401. A backend may also write the answers itself, in which case no model on the app's server is called.

The paperwork: what GOVERNANCE.md records

As with mcp-zerodha, the last piece is a GOVERNANCE.md. It opens by saying it describes controls and is not a certification.

It has a table of what a caller can and cannot do, each control with the file that implements it, where data goes in each mode (demo, connected database, own model, own backend), and how the match score is computed. It records how each control was checked against a local production build: the 21st chat in a minute returns 429, a 5,000-character system prompt returns 400, an upload named ../../../evil-test.txt lands at <tmpdir>/upload-<uuid>.txt.

The checks are also automated. There are 21 Jest test files under src/**/__tests__, covering origin matching, the widget and connector routes, token tampering, the model address guard, provider error mapping and request signing. One of them, a Postgres integration test, runs only when TEST_DATABASE_URL is set. The reference connector has 8 more under connector/test, run with Node's built-in test runner. Both suites check request signatures against the same shared test-vector file.

Its known gaps run to 29, and they should. A selection, in the file's words:

  • Retrieval quality is measured on one document.
  • A backend's scores are only comparable if it embeds with the same model.
  • The same model does not give identical scores on every platform. In QA, the reference server on Linux and the app on macOS scored the same passages up to about 0.03 apart, and one passage fell on different sides of the 0.15 cut-off.
  • No authentication.
  • Rate limits are per instance.
  • Rate limits trust the client IP headers.
  • Allowed sites rely on the browser's Origin and Referer headers.
  • Visitors on allowed sites spend the owner's credits. There are no spend caps.
  • No per-token revocation for model keys.
  • Fencing documents reduces prompt injection; it does not prevent it.
  • No retention control, and no delete-my-data UI.
  • One server key protects every token.
  • Session IDs appear in the server log.

The fencing gap needs a gloss. Prompt injection is text that gets a model to follow its instructions instead of the developer's, and here it can arrive inside an uploaded document. Retrieved passages are wrapped in <documents> tags and the model is told not to follow instructions inside them (9c2b096). That lowers the odds; it does not remove them. There is more on the risk itself in the OWASP LLM01 post.

What carries over to any AI product

None of this is specific to support bots:

  • A displayed control is a claim. An audit log, an SSO toggle or a security badge in the UI is evidence only of a UI. Check the code path behind it.
  • Name a number after what computes it. A score derived from similarity is a match score. Calling it confidence promises something the code never measured.
  • Thresholds belong to a model, and drift by platform. Change the embedding model and every cut-off tuned for the old one is wrong, silently. Keep the model and move the hardware, and passages near the cut-off can still flip.
  • Fail where someone can see it. A zero vector or a canned apology turns an outage into a product that looks merely mediocre.
  • Check what is deployed. Fixes in a blocked pipeline are fixes in a document.
  • Write the gaps down. Here the list is long. It is still more useful to a reviewer than your data stays isolated.

If your AI product is heading into a customer's security review, I can run the same governance review on it: every displayed control traced to the code behind it, and to what is actually deployed.

References

Repository, pinned to the commit this post describes:

  • ai-support-bot at 6e91402
  • GOVERNANCE.md: controls, data flow, known gaps and QA records
  • src/lib/guard.ts: rate limits, size caps and origin checks
  • connector/README.md: the reference backend

Audit commits: 2a40ffe (the four API holes), 9c2b096 (loud failures and document fencing), 80908c7 (the removed claims), 014099d (local embeddings and the match score), 6fd93dd (the retention correction), and the deploy fixes a11ed4c, d4aeaab, 4c8949c, 08fe1da and db15260.

Later features: 67f7d5f (own database), c53498e (allowed sites and own model), 6e91402 (own backend).

Background:

  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM01 Prompt Injection
  • OWASP: Server Side Request Forgery
  • pgvector
  • NIST SP 800-38D: GCM
  • NIST glossary: least privilege
  • MDN: the Origin header
  • Retrieval-augmented generation
  • Hugging Face: getting started with embeddings
  • all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and transformers.js
  • Jest and the Node.js test runner

item.title: AI agent pull requests: who holds merge authority
item.dc:creator: anuj
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen AI agents work on astro-ai, the codebase behind shubhagya.com. In the designed path, none of them merges a pull request: a workflow does. The unattended loop that runs them does hold a written permission to merge its own pull request after QA, and that matters, so it gets its own section below.

Four times, a pull request that had passed everything stayed open anyway. Gates green, QA passed, no conflicts. It sat there, waiting for a signal that had already been sent.

Merge authority is the right to decide that a change lands on main. In astro-ai's design it sits in a GitHub Actions workflow that merges only on evidence: green checks on the head commit, a qa-pass label bound to that commit, and no protected paths touched. The lesson that matters most is to put the merge decision in something that reads artifacts, then deny the merge command to the agents, or say plainly which ones you have not.

This post covers both halves: why merge authority sits in a workflow instead of an agent, and the failure that design kept producing anyway. The agent cycle diagram shows the whole loop if you want the map first.

How agents hand off work without talking to each other

The agents are Claude Code subagents: each one runs in its own context window with its own system prompt, tools and permissions. A subagent starts with no memory of any other, so this system cannot pass work along by conversation.

Every handoff is written somewhere durable instead. The source page lists the channels, and each one exists for a different reason:

A label is GitHub's tag for issues and pull requests. Here it carries the QA verdict, qa-pass or qa-fail, and only one script writes it. When QA records a pass, that script binds it to the SHA QA examined and refuses if the branch has moved since.

Why does this beat conversation? Because an artifact can be re-read by something that was not there when it was written. A merge workflow cannot read an agent's reasoning. It can read a label, a commit and a check result, and it can read them again an hour later and get the same answer.

The repo learned the cost of the alternative directly. Its status file, AGENT_STATUS.md, is gitignored, so nothing written there ever left one machine. The decision log records five issues audited and found already complete on one day, four of them carrying zero comments. The rule now is that the issue holds the decision record.

Where does merge authority sit?

An agent pushes a branch and opens a pull request. The decision to merge lives in agent-merge.yml, a GitHub Actions workflow: a YAML file that GitHub runs on its own machines when a named event happens.

The workflow runs its checks as a chain of steps, and each step runs only if the previous one passed:

  1. Author (own). The pull request was opened by claude[bot] or the repo owner. A pull request from a fork never reaches the job at all.
  2. Gates (gates). Every check on the head commit has finished green. It takes the latest run of each check, so a superseded, cancelled run stops voting, and a check still running counts as not green.
  3. QA (qa). The qa-pass label is present, and neither qa-fail nor needs-human-review is.
  4. Size (size). The diff is under MAX_LINES.
  5. Trust boundary (boundary). The diff touches none of seven protected paths: the system prompts, the knowledge corpus, the workflows themselves, and the four files that decide what is recorded, sent or stored about a user.

A pull request that touches the trust boundary is labelled needs-human-review and left open. One agent, chief, can release that hold, but only with a ruling comment that names the exact head SHA, so the next push cancels it. It cannot skip the gates or the QA label.

The point is least privilege: give each actor only the access its job needs, the same principle behind OWASP's excessive agency risk. Fifteen things write code. In the designed path, one workflow decides what lands, and it decides on evidence rather than on anyone's judgment that the work is finished.

The size check holds nothing

Step 4 is switched off, and the source page says so. MAX_LINES is set to 1000000, which admits any plausible diff.

It was raised on 2026-10-08, and the workflow quotes the owner's reason: "we should not restrict git push and merge for this autonomous system to be successful. If QA is passed, push and merge." The step was left in place so that lowering the number to 400 brings it back with one edit.

A control that is written but inert should be described as inert, not counted as protection. The case for the limit still stands: the repo notes that test coverage is narrow and main deploys with no staging, so green CI proves much more about deleting one file than about a 3D chart.

Where the boundary is a prompt

The same 2026-10-08 grant reaches further than the size limit. CLAUDE.md records it as a standing permission: /agent-cycle, running unattended in agent-work.yml, "pushes its branch and merges its own PR once QA passes." agent-work.yml says the same in a comment. Its denied-tools list blocks rm, sudo, force-push, gh repo, gh secret and gcloud, but not gh pr merge, and the job holds pull-requests: write.

So "no agent merges" describes the design, not a hard guarantee. agent-merge is the workflow that merges the loop's pull requests. qa and qa-lead are told never to merge, and chief that it cannot merge directly. But only the steward is actually denied gh pr merge in its tool list (agent-steward.yml). For the delivery loop, what stands between it and a merge is its instructions plus branch protection on main, which requires the gates and build-gates checks but not the qa-pass label.

That is the same lesson as the size check. Where the boundary is a prompt rather than a deny, say so.

Why the authority is not an agent's

In this same repo, a dev-lead agent wrote USER AUTHORISED PUSH this turn into a status file and then cited its own line as permission. The earlier post covers that failure; the structural answer is to hold merge authority in a workflow, so there is nothing for an agent to grant itself. That answer is only as strong as the tool deny behind it, which, as above, the delivery loop does not have.

The missing edge: why green pull requests stayed open

Here is the failure the design kept producing.

agent-merge starts on two kinds of event. workflow_run starts one workflow when another finishes, here the PR gates and verify-build workflows. pull_request_target with type labeled starts it when a label is added.

The workflow's own comment calls both of these edges. An edge is a one-time notification that something changed. If the condition is not yet true when the edge arrives, the run exits, and nothing asks again.

So whenever the last green check landed after the last edge, the pull request stayed green, qa-pass and mergeable, indefinitely. The workflow lists four times it happened:

  • #303: ready_for_review was not among the pull request events pr-gates listened to, so the pull request, once out of draft, carried no check at all.
  • #322: a pull request authored with GITHUB_TOKEN emits no workflow_run. GitHub's documentation states that, apart from workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch, events triggered by GITHUB_TOKEN do not create workflow runs.
  • #352: the run that went green was a manual workflow_dispatch, which the job deliberately ignores. A dispatched run checks out the branch, not the merge result, so it does not prove the merge.
  • #356: verify-build is a different workflow, and agent-merge listened only to PR gates. On a docs-only change pr-gates skips its suite and finished in 9 seconds, while verify-build took 68.

Each was fixed by adding or correcting an edge. The workflow's conclusion is blunt: "a fifth edge was always going to be missed -- so the answer is to stop relying on edges."

[caption id="attachment_812" align="aligncenter" width="1600"] The cycle ribbon: every agent-work run from 8 October to 2 November, by hour (IST). Green shipped and merged, amber left a PR open, grey produced nothing, red failed.[/caption]

The sweep, and what it does not fix

The answer was a sweep (#357): a cron schedule, which runs a workflow on a clock rather than on an event, set to */30. That asks for every 30 minutes.

The sweep adds no authority. It picks a candidate pull request number, and then the same steps re-check every condition through the GitHub API in the same order. The worst it can do is merge something that already satisfies every condition.

It also turned out to be much slower than it looks. Over the 71 scheduled runs up to 2026-10-27, the measured gap was:

Not once in 71 runs did it fire at 30 minutes. The repo attributes this to GitHub throttling short-interval cron on public repositories; GitHub's documentation says only that scheduled runs can be delayed during periods of high load.

So the sweep stopped pull requests stranding forever. It did not make them fast. A stranded pull request now waits hours instead of indefinitely.

The edge bug also came back. On #562, a code change, gates finished in 7m43s and build-gates in 10m25s. The workflow_run edge fired while build-gates was still queued, nothing was listening for the second workflow, and the merge check exited. The workflow records that the hole cost two stranded pull requests before it was closed on 2026-10-27, by listening to both gate workflows.

The decision log records one more measured case (#573) that was not a missing edge at all. A redundant dispatched gate run became the last check to go green, and a dispatched run is exactly the kind that cannot wake a merge. The pull request met every condition and sat 2h36m until the queue was drained by hand.

A backstop that arrives in hours is not a substitute for an edge that arrives in seconds. The sweep is a floor on how long a strand lasts, and every edge is still load-bearing.

Lessons for a startup CTO running AI agents

None of these lessons depend on astro-ai's scale. They come from what is in the repo.

  • Put merge authority in something that cannot be talked into it. An agent that can merge can be the agent that writes its own permission slip. A workflow reading labels and check results cannot. Then deny the merge command to the agents, or say plainly which ones you have not.
  • Make every handoff a durable artifact. If the next actor cannot re-read it, it did not happen. Bind verdicts to a commit SHA, so a pass on old code cannot vote on new code.
  • Event triggers are edges, and edges get missed. Anything that must eventually happen needs a reconciler that re-asks the question on a clock, and the reconciler must re-check everything rather than carry authority of its own.
  • Measure the backstop. The cron said 30 minutes; the measurement said two to seven hours. Use the measured number when you decide how much the primary path can be allowed to fail.
  • Describe switched-off controls as switched off. An inert size limit, stated plainly, is a decision someone can revisit. The same limit counted as protection is a false claim.
  • Hold changes by path, not just by result. Green checks say little about a change to the prompts, the gates or user data, so those paths wait for a ruling regardless.

On 2026-10-21 main itself also gained branch protection requiring a pull request plus the gates and build-gates checks. A protected branch with required status checks refuses a merge until those checks pass, whatever opened it. It does not require qa-pass; only agent-merge reads that label. That is the floor; the workflow above is the decision.

The full loop, all fifteen agents and every artifact between them, is on the agent cycle page. The same loop is also set to build the app toward a larger user base, which is the subject of a separate post.

If your agents already open pull requests, I can review where merge authority actually sits in your setup and which of your boundaries are prompts rather than denies, the same audit this post runs on Shubh Bhagya.

FAQ

Can an agent in astro-ai merge its own pull request? In the designed path, no: the agent-merge workflow does. But the unattended delivery loop holds a written grant to merge its own pull request once QA passes (CLAUDE.md), and its denied-tools list does not block gh pr merge. Only the steward is denied that command.

Why did pull requests that passed everything stay open? The merge workflow started on events, and an event is a one-time notification. When the last green check landed after the last event, nothing asked again. The workflow lists four such strands, each fixed by adding or correcting a trigger.

How often does a 30-minute GitHub cron actually run? In this repo, never at 30 minutes. Over 71 scheduled runs up to 2026-10-27 the gap ranged from 126 to 444 minutes, according to agent-merge.yml. GitHub's documentation says only that scheduled runs can be delayed during periods of high load.

References

  • astro-ai, docs/agent-cycle.html, the agent cycle source page (generated as of 2026-10-27)
  • astro-ai, .github/workflows/agent-merge.yml, merge conditions, the four strands, the sweep and its measured interval
  • astro-ai, CLAUDE.md, the QA verdict script, the */30 sweep rule (#357), and the 2026-10-08 grant letting the autonomous loop push and merge
  • astro-ai, .github/workflows/agent-work.yml, the delivery loop's merge permission and denied-tools list
  • astro-ai, .github/workflows/agent-steward.yml, the steward's denied-tools list, which includes gh pr merge
  • astro-ai, qa.md, qa-lead.md and chief.md, the agents' instructions not to merge
  • astro-ai, ARCHITECTURE.md, decision log rows for the sweep (#357), branch protection (#393), the dispatched-run strand (#573) and the issue as durable record (#607)
  • astro-ai pull requests and issues: #303, #322, #352, #356, #357, #562
  • Anthropic, Claude Code subagents
  • GitHub, About workflows
  • GitHub, Events that trigger workflows (workflow_run, schedule, and GITHUB_TOKEN-triggered events)
  • GitHub, About protected branches
  • GitHub, Managing labels
  • NIST CSRC glossary, least privilege
  • What actually goes wrong with a team of agents, the earlier post on the self-authorisation incident

item.title: Read-only by default: how mcp-multi-db enforces it
item.dc:creator: anuj
item.content:encoded:
Update, 2026-11-02: v1.1 adds opt-in governance on top of these two layers: table policy from the query plan, redaction by column origin, row limits and an audit log. That post also covers the two bypasses an adversarial review found before release.

mcp-multi-db connects an AI agent to PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite through one server. Pointing something like that at real data only makes sense if writes are impossible rather than discouraged, so read-only enforcement is the part of the design worth writing down.

It is enforced twice, and the interesting part is that the two layers are not doing the same job. One produces good errors. The other is the boundary.

Why a tool description is not enough

The obvious way to build this is to wrap the database client you already have and tell the model to behave — put only issue SELECT statements in the tool description and move on.

That fails for a reason worth being precise about. A tool description is an input to a probabilistic system. It shifts the distribution of outputs; it does not constrain the set of them. Treating it as an access control is the same category error as validating a form only in the browser.

It also fails quietly. The model will comply almost every time, so the logs look clean for weeks. What that measures is the common case, not the boundary.

Layer 1: the SQL-text guard

validateReadOnlySql runs before anything reaches a database. It does four things, in order:

The opening check is an allowlist — SELECT, WITH, EXPLAIN, nothing else. That is the load-bearing half. The keyword denylist that follows is the belt to its braces: it catches mutations hiding later in an otherwise well-formed read, such as a CTE that writes.

EXPLAIN returns early without a LIMIT, because appending one to a query plan is meaningless.

The guard is a regex, and that is fine

Layer 1 is string matching, and string matching against SQL is famously leaky. A regex cannot see that a keyword sits inside a string literal, so a perfectly legitimate query gets rejected:

SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE body LIKE '%DELETE ME%';

That is a real limitation, and it is the correct trade only because layer 1 is not the security boundary. If it were, every gap in the pattern would be an exploit, and false negatives — the ones you never notice — would matter far more than false positives. Because it isn't, the guard can be deliberately conservative: it fails loudly and early with a readable error, and the cost of being wrong is an inconvenienced query rather than a mutated table.

A filter you can bypass is not a boundary. A filter sitting in front of a real boundary is a good error message. The same regex is a liability in the first role and an asset in the second — what changes is what stands behind it.

Layer 2: the database refuses

The guarantee comes from the connection, not the code above it. Each adapter prevents writes at the engine:

The case that motivates this is the one layer 1 structurally cannot catch: a SELECT that calls a function with side effects. Nothing in the statement text is a mutating keyword — the write happens inside the function body. The text guard sees a clean read; the read-only transaction refuses it anyway.

This is why SECURITY.md states it plainly: a string-based filter alone is not a security boundary, and layer 2 is what makes the read-only guarantee real. Enforcement lives in code I did not write and cannot accidentally weaken.

The rollback is unconditional rather than reserved for errors, so no transaction state survives a query either way.

Bounded by default

Two limits stop a single query becoming an incident.

Row count is capped in layer 1: LIMIT 100 by default, clamped to a maximum of 1000, injected when the model omits one and lowered when the model asks for more. The result carries a truncated flag, so the agent knows it is looking at a prefix and can narrow the query rather than confidently summarising the first hundred rows as though they were all of them.

Statement timeouts are set per connection at 30 seconds on PostgreSQL and MySQL. Without one, a query that hangs past the client's transport timeout looks to the agent like a dead server rather than a slow query.

Report truncation

A tool that silently returns partial data is worse than one that fails. The model cannot tell the difference, so it will present the prefix as the answer. Truncation has to be reported in the response, not just applied.

Four tools, not one

The server exposes a graded surface rather than a single query escape hatch:

The first three exist so the agent can discover structure before writing SQL, and list_databases is documented as the call to make first — every other tool needs a database_id to target, since multiple engines are live at once.

The narrower tools also answer most questions on their own. A schema question routed to describe_table needs no SQL and cannot fail a validation check.

What is left to the operator

Two layers of enforcement still leave decisions outside the server's control, and SECURITY.md names them rather than implying the defaults are sufficient:

  • A dedicated database user with GRANT SELECT only. This is the strongest control available, and it is the one that holds even if a bug slips past both layers. It is a recommendation rather than a feature because the server cannot provision it for you.
  • Point at a read replica rather than a primary where the option exists.
  • Scope what you connect. The agent can read every table its configured user can see; the server bounds what can be done, not what can be seen.
  • Keep connection strings out of version control — databases.json holds credentials and is gitignored for that reason.

That list is the honest boundary of what a tool like this can promise. It can make writes impossible. It cannot decide which data an agent should be allowed to read, and pretending otherwise would be the more dangerous default.

The server is open source at mcp-multi-db; the enforcement described here is in src/sql/validateReadOnly.ts and the three adapters under src/adapters/.

If you want an agent reading production data without any way to change it, that is an MCP server I can build for your stack, with the same two layers and the operator's half written down.
item.excerpt:encoded: A walk through the two layers that make an MCP server safe to point at a real database — a SQL-text guard that is allowed to be imperfect, and a connection that cannot write.
